[[File:Automedian triangle.svg|thumb|240px|An automedian triangle (black) with side lengths in the proportion 13:17:7, its three [[Median (geometry)|medians]] (brown), and a triangle [[Similarity (geometry)|similar]] to the original one whose sides are translated copies of the medians]]
In [[plane geometry]], an '''automedian triangle''' is a [[triangle]] in which the lengths of the three [[Median (geometry)|medians]] (the line segments connecting each [[vertex (geometry)|vertex]] to the midpoint of the opposite side) are proportional to the lengths of the three sides, in a different order. The three medians of an automedian triangle may be [[translation (geometry)|translated]] to form the sides of a second triangle that is [[Similarity (geometry)|similar]] to the first one.

==Characterization==
The side lengths of an automedian triangle satisfy the formula <math>2a^2=b^2+c^2</math> or a permutation thereof, analogous to the [[Pythagorean theorem]] characterizing [[right triangle]]s as the triangles satisfying the formula <math>a^2+b^2=c^2</math>.

Equivalently, in order for the three numbers <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math> to be the sides of an automedian triangle, the sequence of three squared side lengths <math>b^2</math>, <math>a^2</math>, and <math>c^2</math> should form an [[arithmetic progression]].<ref name="dickson">{{citation|title=History of the Theory of Numbers, Volume II: Diophantine Analysis|title-link=History of the Theory of Numbers|first=Leonard Eugene|last=Dickson|authorlink=Leonard Eugene Dickson|publisher=Carnegie Institution of Washington|year=1920|contribution=Three squares in arithmetical progression {{math|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''z''<sup>2</sup> = 2''y''<sup>2</sup>}}|contribution-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uiuo.ark:/13960/t59d9qq13&seq=467|pages=435–440}}.</ref> That is, <math>b^2-k = a^2</math>, and <math>a^2-k = c^2</math> (for example, if <math>b=17</math>, <math>a=13</math>, and <math>c=7</math>, then <math>k=120</math>: <math>17^2-120 = 13^2 = 169</math>, and <math>13^2-120 = 7^2 = 49</math>).

==Construction from right triangles==
If <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, and <math>z</math> are the three sides of a right triangle, sorted in increasing order by size, and if <math>2x<z</math>, then <math>z</math>, <math>x+y</math>, and <math>y-x</math> are the three sides of an automedian triangle. For instance, the right triangle with side lengths 5, 12, and 13 can be used to form in this way an automedian triangle with side lengths 13, 17, and 7.<ref name="parry">{{citation
 | last = Parry | first = C. F.
 | issue = 472
 | journal = The Mathematical Gazette
 | jstor = 3620241
 | pages = 151–154
 | title = Steiner–Lehmus and the automedian triangle
 | volume = 75
 | year = 1991| doi = 10.2307/3620241
 }}.</ref>

The condition that <math>2x<z</math> is necessary: if it were not met, then the three numbers <math>a=z</math>, <math>b=x+y</math>, and <math>c=y-x</math> would still satisfy the equation <math>2a^2=b^2+c^2</math> characterizing automedian triangles, but they would not satisfy the [[triangle inequality]] and could not be used to form the sides of a triangle.

Consequently, using [[Pythagorean_triple#Proof_of_Euclid.27s_formula|Euler's formula]] that generates primitive [[Pythagorean triangle]]s it is possible to generate primitive ''integer'' automedian triangles (i.e., with the sides sharing no common factor) as
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
a&=m^2+n^2\\
b&=m^2+2mn-n^2\\
c&=|m^2-2mn-n^2|\\
\end{align}</math>
with <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> coprime, <math>m+n</math> odd, and to satisfy the triangle inequality <math>n<m<n\sqrt{3}</math> (if the quantity inside the [[absolute value]] signs is negative) or <math>m>(2+\sqrt{3})n</math> (if that quantity is positive). Then this triangle's medians <math> t_a, t_b, t_c</math> are found by using the above expressions for its sides in the general [[median (geometry)#Formulas involving the medians' lengths|formula for medians]]:
<math display=block>t_a = \sqrt {\frac{2 b^2 + 2 c^2 - a^2}{4} }= \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad t_b = \sqrt {\frac{2 a^2 + 2 c^2 - b^2}{4} }= \frac{c\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad t_c = \sqrt {\frac{2 a^2 + 2 b^2 - c^2}{4} }= \frac{b\sqrt{3}}{2},</math>
where the second equation in each case reflects the automedian feature <math>2a^2=b^2+c^2.</math>

From this can be seen the similarity relationships 
<math display=block>\frac{t_a}{t_b}=\frac{a}{c}, \qquad \frac{t_b}{t_c}=\frac{c}{b}, \qquad \frac{t_c}{t_a}=\frac{b}{a} \qquad \text{and hence} \qquad t_a  :  t_b  :  t_c \quad = \quad a  :  c :  b.</math>

There is a primitive integer-sided automedian triangle that is not generated from a right triangle: namely, the [[equilateral triangle]] with sides of unit length.

==Additional properties==

If <math>\Delta (a,b,c)</math> is the area of the automedian triangle, by [[Heron's formula]] <math>\Delta (t_a,t_b,t_c) =(3/4)\Delta (a,b,c).</math><ref>Benyi, Arpad, "A Heron-type formula for the triangle", ''Mathematical Gazette'' 87, July 2003, 324–326.</ref>

The [[Euler line]] of an automedian triangle is perpendicular to the median to side <math>a</math>.<ref name=parry/>

If the medians of an automedian triangle are extended to the [[circumcircle]] of the triangle, then the three points <math>LMN</math> where the extended medians meet the circumcircle form an [[isosceles triangle]]. The triangles for which this second triangle <math>LMN</math> is isosceles are exactly the triangles that are themselves either isosceles or automedian. This property of automedian triangles stands in contrast to the [[Steiner–Lehmus theorem]], according to which the only triangles two of whose [[angle bisector]]s have equal length are the isosceles triangles.<ref name="parry"/>

Additionally, suppose that <math>ABC</math> is an automedian triangle, in which vertex <math>A</math> stands opposite the side <math>a</math>. Let <math>G</math> be the point where the three medians of <math>ABC</math> intersect, and let <math>AL</math> be one of the extended medians of <math>ABC</math>, with <math>L</math> lying on the circumcircle of <math>ABC</math>. Then <math>BGCL</math> is a [[parallelogram]], the two triangles <math>BGL</math> and <math>CLG</math> into which it may be subdivided are both similar to <math>ABC</math>, <math>G</math> is the midpoint of <math>AL</math>, and the [[Euler line]] of the triangle is the [[perpendicular bisector]] of <math>AL</math>.<ref name="parry"/>

When generating a primitive automedian triangle from a primitive [[Pythagorean triple]] using the Euclidean parameters <math>m,n</math>, then <math>m>n</math> and it follows that <math>b \ge a \ge c</math>. As non-primitive automedian triangles are multiples of their primitives the inequalities of the sides apply to all integer automedian triangles. Equality occurs only for trivial equilateral triangles. Furthermore, because <math>m+n</math> is always odd, all the sides <math>a,b,c</math> have to be odd. This fact allows automedian triples to have sides and perimeter of prime numbers only. For example, (13, 17, 7) has perimeter 37.

Because in a primitive automedian triangle side <math>a</math> is the sum of two squares and equal to the hypotenuse of the generating primitive Pythagorean triple, it is divisible only by primes congruent to 1&nbsp;(mod 4). Consequently, <math>a</math> must be congruent to 1&nbsp;(mod 4).

Similarly, because the sides are related by <math>2a^2=b^2+c^2</math>, each of the sides <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> in the primitive automedian is the difference between twice a square and a square. They are also the sum and difference of the legs of a primitive Pythagorean triple. This constrains <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> to be divisible only by primes congruent to ±1&nbsp;(mod 8). Consequently, <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> must be congruent to ±1&nbsp;(mod 8).<ref>{{cite OEIS |A001132 |mode=cs2}}</ref>

==History==
The study of integer squares in arithmetic progression has a long history stretching back to [[Diophantus]] and [[Fibonacci]]; it is closely connected with [[Congruum|congrua]], which are the numbers that can be the differences of the squares in such a progression.<ref name="dickson"/> However, the connection between this problem and automedian triangles is much more recent. The problem of characterizing automedian triangles was posed in the late 19th century in the ''Educational Times'' (in French) by [[Joseph Jean Baptiste Neuberg]], and solved there with the formula <math>2a^2=b^2+c^2</math> by [[William John Greenstreet]].<ref>{{citation|title=Mathematical Questions and Solutions from the "Educational Times", Volume I|publisher=F. Hodgson|year=1902|pages=77–78|contribution=Problem 12705|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LdIGAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA77}}. Originally published in the ''Educational Times'' 71 (1899), p. 56</ref>

==Special cases==
Apart from the trivial cases of equilateral triangles, the triangle with side lengths 17, 13, and 7 is the smallest (by area or perimeter) automedian triangle with integer side lengths.<ref name="parry"/>

There is only one automedian right triangle, the triangle with side lengths proportional to 1, the [[square root of 2]], and the [[square root of 3]].<ref name="parry"/> This triangle is the second triangle in the [[spiral of Theodorus]]. It is the only right triangle in which two of the medians are perpendicular to each other.<ref name="parry"/>
